title: Doing The Right Thing: Accountability In The Age Of AI Coding Summary
gist: InfoQ Engineering Culture podcast in which Hugo Venturini (ex-Meta, ex-Qwant CTO) argues humans remain accountable for AI-written code, that PR bloat predates AI and should be handled with trust-based selective review, and that AI's collapse of PM/architect/tester roles will only raise quality (as Microsoft's 2014 dev/test merge did) if organisations build blame-free, transparent cultures and teach engineers to ask better questions.

insights.claim: Hugo Venturini argues AI is just another, very powerful, tool and that the human directing it remains accountable for whatever goes wrong, rejecting the 'the agent did this' excuse.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Liability and quality ownership for AI-written software stays with engineering orgs, not tool vendors; governance tooling around accountability has a market.
insights.quote: And yet if it fails, the one conducting this great tool is accountable, is in charge and should answer what goes wrong.

insights.claim: Venturini says that code generation must be exact to the character, and that proper tooling can make the AI loop on feedback so that much of what can be automated is already done before output returns to the human.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Validation/feedback-loop harnesses (compile, test, verify) are the value layer around coding agents — the category his own startup works in.
insights.quote: when you want to generate code, code has to be to the colon, to the semi-colon, to the character.

insights.claim: Venturini, who still reports 'wow moments' with AI at least weekly, defines 'doing the right thing' as solving the user's problem, with each step of the chain (product decision, coding, testing, release) having its own right thing.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Frames AI evaluation around end-user outcomes per pipeline stage rather than raw code output.

themes.theme: Code review scale and pull-request bloat

insights.claim: Large pull requests predate AI; Venturini says the review-scale problem existed before and teams should first ask whether everything needs review at all if code compiles, passes tests and behaves as intended.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the narrative that AI uniquely broke code review; demand for review tooling may be about volume, not novelty.
insights.quote: the size of pull request is a problem which does not rise with AI. It was already existing before.

insights.claim: Interviewer Shane Hastie cites reports of 2,000-line pull requests and a senior engineer with a backlog of over 300 pull requests, each hundreds of lines long, awaiting review.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Anecdotal signal of review bottlenecks created by AI-accelerated code output, a pain point for dev-tool vendors to target.

insights.claim: Venturini's team does not review every diff: trusted engineers merge boilerplate themselves and remain accountable for fixes, while review is proactively requested for the core of the product for quality and knowledge sharing.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Trust-based selective review is one practical answer to AI-driven diff volume, reducing reliance on universal human review.
insights.locator: Second thing is, already before as well

insights.claim: Venturini dismisses giant single-diff AI rewrites as 'just for the show' and says skill now lies in getting AI to produce a proper stack of small diffs so only the product's heart needs review.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Stacked-diff workflows and AI that decomposes changes may matter more than AI that produces huge changes.
insights.quote: "Look, I have rewritten this entire big product in only one diff", which is just for the show. Let's face it, nobody does this.

insights.claim: Venturini admits he has no good answer to the problem of the sheer number of AI-generated diffs and calls it an open industry question.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Unsolved diff-volume review is an open opportunity for tooling (prioritisation, automated verification).
insights.quote: How do you review for number of diffs? I don't have any good answer
insights.locator: How do you review for number of diffs?

themes.theme: Quality lessons from Microsoft's dev/test merge

insights.claim: Venturini recounts that when Microsoft merged its software engineer and tester branches in 2014, removing the separate testing step actually raised software quality because engineers became accountable for the whole product.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that consolidating roles can raise quality when accountability consolidates too.
insights.quote: By removing the official testing step by somebody else, it actually raised the quality of the software.
insights.locator: I got a story about rising quality

insights.claim: Venturini argues AI is again merging roles—everyone becomes a tester of AI-written code—but quality is not yet rising because people blame the AI rather than feeling accountable for the tool's output.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: If accountability lags, AI-heavy shops may ship lower-quality software, a risk to product reputation and a driver for QA/verification spend.
insights.quote: we don't see an increase of quality yet, and I believe it's because people are still blaming the AI and don't feel accountable

insights.claim: Venturini says he has noticed software he uses lacking quality over recent months and links it to press reports that those vendors use AI massively.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Early anecdotal sign that heavy AI adoption can degrade perceived product quality — a watch item for vendors marketing AI-built software.

themes.theme: AI collapses role boundaries; seniority = asking right questions

insights.claim: Venturini argues AI shrinks organisations back toward startup-like generalism where an engineer acts as PM, architect and tester, but people who have never done those jobs misunderstand them.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: AI-enabled role collapse implies smaller teams and changes headcount mix across PM/QA/architecture functions.

insights.claim: Venturini says AI always answers the question asked, so it barely helps people who ask the wrong questions, and seniority is precisely the ability to ask questions that move toward a solution.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Value of AI is gated by user expertise; senior talent becomes more, not less, valuable and training is a needed investment.
insights.quote: It always answers the question you're asking, but if you're asking the wrong questions and being a senior is asking the right questions
insights.locator: And when the AI comes, it really helps you

insights.claim: Venturini calls for more training to help people ask AI better questions, since AI empowers people to do things they are not sure how to do.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Demand for AI-literacy and role-crossing training inside engineering orgs.
insights.locator: And when the AI comes, it really helps you

themes.theme: Psychological safety and transparency as accountability enablers

insights.claim: Venturini argues people only dare to take accountability if they know they will be accountable but not blamed; giving tooling without that psychological safety achieves nothing.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: AI tooling ROI depends on organisational culture; tool rollouts in fear-driven orgs underperform.
insights.quote: People dare to do things if they know they will be accountable but not blamed for what happens.
insights.locator: Asking the Right Questions: Shifting Further Left

insights.claim: As CTO of Qwant, a 90-person organisation, Venturini fixed a culture where people would 'lie, hide, steal' by leading by example with weekly open Q&As, admitting mistakes, and naming solutions rather than people.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Concrete playbook for turnaround of a broken engineering culture; leadership transparency as a lever.
insights.quote: People would lie, hide, steal, everything was wrong.
insights.locator: I'm not sure that the recipe

insights.claim: Venturini's Q&A initially drew only easy questions until he introduced an anonymous question board routed through other managers, after which people voted and stacked difficult questions ahead of sessions.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Anonymity mechanisms surface hard truths that leadership otherwise misses.

insights.claim: Venturini holds that making mistakes is acceptable but repeating them is not, and that culture change requires patience because human results lag compared with software.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Culture transformations take time; expect lagged returns on org-change investments.
insights.quote: What is not acceptable is repeating your own mistakes because you have not learned

themes.theme: Leading change below the top and IC influence

insights.claim: Venturini says culture change can start at team level: at a roughly 1,200-person scale-up he found two teams already practising transparency and accountability, with less org-wide impact but real results.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Bottom-up cultural practices can spread through manager networks without top-down mandates.
insights.locator: Leading Culture Change at Any Level

insights.claim: Venturini argues managers belong to two teams—their own and the team of managers—with sometimes opposing goals, and must think beyond their own team; toxic management is devastating because managers amplify impact either way.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Management quality is a leveraged variable in org performance, positive or negative.
insights.locator: And that's the difficulty of being a manager

insights.claim: Venturini observes that ICs with manager-level influence are technically strong, humble and listen more than they speak, and that many of the best staff and principal engineers had tried management and returned.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Supports dual-track careers and manager-IC pendulum moves as a source of senior talent.
insights.quote: they were always, always listening more than they were speaking

insights.claim: Venturini recommends swinging between IC and manager roles, as he did across Microsoft, Facebook, his own company and a CTO role, because it builds understanding of the full scope of building products for users.
insights.speaker: Hugo Venturini
insights.so_what: Career fluidity builds the product-wide judgement that AI-era role collapse demands.
insights.locator: So I would say give it a go
